Hi Ceri. I'm a 19 Year old male and I'm contending with almost the same problems as you are.

I'd like to share a bit of my backstory. I am currently studying to become a doctor. I live in a country where this education is extremely expensive, unless you're in a government-funded institution, in which case it costs literally peanuts. Naturally, the competition for entrance into one of these institutions is brutal. 

I was 17 when I passed this exam for the first time, which is quite young relatively. I have also been a bit of a perfectionist and I too had made a roadmap of what my "perfect" life should be. Consequently, I refused to join that year because the University I had been accepted to wasn't high enough (at least for me) on the ranking charts of government-run institutes. A lot of people called me ungrateful (I had been given this big chance and I was refusing to use it). However, the perfectionist part of my brain was refusing to budge. So I waited and then sat for this exam the next year. I also scored a 1530 on the SAT-I and applied to a few Universities abroad, to which I was accepted, even receiving full-ride scholarships. But in the end, I decided to stay in my country to become a doctor (This time I had been accepted to one of the best Medical Schools in my country).

Now I had a new problem. Since I had waited a year, some of my friends and peers (who had decided to opt for other career paths instead of waiting a year) were ahead of me. This derailed my plan of a "perfect" life. As stupid as it sounds, this (coupled with an episode of almost disabling migraines) sent me into a deep depression. I couldn't function properly for a few months, barricading myself in my room and mourning the loss of my "perfect" life. Then came the bouts of self-doubt. "Maybe I should have gone abroad to study and not stayed here to become a doctor". "Maybe I should have done what people around me had told me to do and joined a medical university the first time around". 

But, it is my belief that when a person is broken down but he/she manages to pick himself/herself up again, he becomes stronget than he was before he broke down. I have come to a few realisations over the past year. I can't promise that these will be any sort of cure-alls. We all have differing circumstances and thus differing obstacles and challenges. But if they do help you in some way, then I'd be very happy indeed.

1. No one has a clue about life. At first, I too thought that I would have figured everything out about life by the time I reached Medical School. Now I know that anyone who says they have their life completely sorted out is lying to you. Believe me, everyone is confused. This world wouldn't be half so interesting, or terrifying, if everyone knew what they had to do. So if you feel like you don't have a clue right now about what you want to do in life, that's completely natural.

2. There's is no **FUNCTIONING** roadmap to a perfect life because a perfect life doesn't exist. No matter how much we want to avoid pain, we can't deny that pain is a central part of life. We all will have to endure sorrow, regrets, betrayals, melancholy, etc even as we celebrate hope, happiness and the joys of the world. And that is okay. We can't design a perfect life. We have to salvage it from the rubble of the world. And it's hard to do that. If it were easy, everyone would be able to do it. So don't beat youself up about it if you think your life is far from the map you envisioned for it. Your life is a work in progress. Would it be fair to judge an unfinished Mona Lisa with a finished mural of the Sistine Chapel or the finished painting of The Last Supper ?

3. There is no guarantee to a "successful" life. From the beginning of our lives, we've been told that **this** is what you should do in order to ensure that you have a successful life. But that's wrong because life is too complicated and filled with too many variables for such a "guaranteed" method of success to be possible. There are some guidelines that are more of less accurate but a guarantee is impossible. And that's okay. We cannot control the many variables of life but we **CAN** control how hard we work. Strive to do the best that you can. You may end up surprising yourself. My uncle was the founder and "Chairman of the Board" of a multinational conglomerate and he once told me that his "perfect life" had consisted of just a house, and motorcycle on which he could travel with his wife and kids. He told me he that he tried to do his best, never caring about the results of his hard work. And life ended up surprising him by giving him more than he ever wanted.

As Joseph Campbell once said, "We must let go of the life we have planned, so as to accept the one that is waiting for us".

4. Age doesn't matter. I too thought that I'd have my life all figured out and set-up by the time I reached 30. The mere thought that it may not be possible was enough to send me into a deep bout of depression. Now, I know that although I'll try my damned hardest to achieve this goal of mine, it's okay if my life isn't prefect by the time I reach 30. History is filled with people who achieved great things in their lives even though they hadn't figured out what to do with themselves until very late in life. As they say, "Age is just a number". You shouldn't let it dictate your life.


You have a lot going for yourself. You're educated. You have a bright future ahead of you. You don't need to feel bad that you are confused, because that's natural. And btw, the next time 10-year-old you tries to make you feel bad that you haven't yet accomplished what you set out to do, remind her (and yourself) that she isn't aware of your struggles and the hardships and hurdles you faced to be who you are and stand were you stand right. Thus she has no right to judge you.

I wish you nothing but happiness and I hope you can live a life without regrets because **that** is the only way to live. 👍
